# What this vignette covers

Counts from neighboring survey points often resemble each other more than the
landscape covariates can explain. This leftover pattern is residual spatial
autocorrelation. A model that ignores it tends to report standard errors that
are too small, and it can distort the estimated scale of effect. This vignette
shows how to estimate scales of effect while a spatial field in the regression
model absorbs that pattern.

You will simulate counts with a known scale of effect and a known field, fit
the model with and without the field, read both sets of estimates, and predict
at survey points, at new locations, and across a map. Read
`vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` first. The field is fitted by
`glmmTMB`, a package that `multiScaleR` suggests but does not install, and the
code below runs only when `glmmTMB` is available.

```{r no-glmmTMB-note, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !has_glmmTMB}
cat("> **Note.** `glmmTMB` was not available when this vignette was built, so",
    "the code is shown without its results.")
```

# Know what a spatial field does

A spatial field is a random effect with one value per survey location, where
values at nearby locations are correlated and the correlation fades with
distance. It stands in for spatially structured drivers that you did not
measure. Add one when the residuals of an ordinary model are similar at
neighboring points.

The field has a distance parameter of its own, the range. Do not confuse it
with the scale of effect.

| | Scale of effect (sigma) | Field range |
|:--|:--|:--|
| What it describes | How far the landscape around a point influences the response | How far apart two points can be while their unexplained variation stays correlated |
| What it acts on | One landscape covariate | The part of the response the covariates leave unexplained |
| How to treat it | The ecological result. Report it as an effective distance | A nuisance parameter that describes the residual pattern |

# Simulate counts with a known field

The counts bundled with the package were simulated without a spatial field, so
they cannot show what a field changes. This example keeps the bundled
landscape and survey points and simulates new counts. The true scales of effect
stay at 250 m for `land1` and 500 m for `land2`. The field has a standard
deviation of 0.6 on the log scale and a range of 800 m.

```{r simulate}
data("surv_pts")
pts <- vect(surv_pts)      # 100 survey points
xy  <- crds(pts)           # their coordinates, in meters
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))

# Landscape covariates smoothed at the true scales, then standardized
truth  <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast[[c("land1", "land2")]],
                              sigma = c(250, 500), kernel = "gaussian",
                              verbose = FALSE)
x_true <- scale(as.matrix(extract(truth, pts, ID = FALSE)))

set.seed(1)
# The field: correlation between two points is exp(-distance / 800)
d_mat <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
field <- drop(t(chol(0.6^2 * exp(-d_mat / 800))) %*% rnorm(nrow(xy)))
site  <- rnorm(nrow(xy))   # a covariate measured at the survey point

# Log expected count: intercept, site effect, landscape effects, and the field
log_mu <- 1 + 0.3 * site - 0.5 * x_true[, "land1"] +
  0.7 * x_true[, "land2"] + field
dat <- data.frame(counts = rpois(nrow(xy), exp(log_mu)), site = site)
```

```{r use-stored-data, include = FALSE}
# The stored fit used these simulated values. Fall back on the stored copy if
# a platform difference in random number generation changed anything.
if (!isTRUE(all.equal(dat, field_cache$dat))) dat <- field_cache$dat
```

# Fit the model without a field

Start with the ordinary workflow from the Quick Start, which gives the baseline
for the comparison.

```{r fit-glm}
# bin = TRUE stores distance-binned summaries, which speed up every refit
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast, max_D = 1700,
                      kernel = "gaussian", bin = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
df <- data.frame(dat, inputs$kernel_dat)

start_glm <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)
fit_glm   <- multiScale_optim(start_glm, inputs, n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)
```

# Add a spatial field

`glmmTMB` writes a spatial field as a covariance term in the model formula. The
term needs two columns. The first holds the coordinates of each row, built with
`glmmTMB::numFactor()`. The second is a grouping factor with a single level,
which tells `glmmTMB` that every point belongs to one shared field.

```{r start-field}
df$pos <- glmmTMB::numFactor(xy[, 1], xy[, 2])   # coordinates, in meters
df$grp <- factor(rep("all", nrow(df)))           # one field for all points

# exp() here is glmmTMB's exponential covariance, not the exponential function
start_field <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  counts ~ site + land1 + land2 + exp(pos + 0 | grp),
  family = poisson(), data = df,
  start  = list(theta = c(log(0.5), log(500)))   # log field SD, log range (m)
)
```

**Choosing `start`:** Supply starting values for the field. By default
`glmmTMB` starts the range at one coordinate unit, here 1 m. No two survey
points are correlated at that range, so the optimizer cannot move and the fit
fails its convergence check. `multiScale_optim()` then returns the starting
sigma values with no standard errors, and it warns that the search never left
its start. Start the range at or above the spacing
between neighboring points, which is about 310 m here.

Use projected coordinates in the same distance units as the raster, because the
range is estimated in those units and nothing is rescaled for you.

Pass the starting model to `multiScale_optim()` as usual. The default
`backend = "refit"` refits the `glmmTMB` model at each candidate scale, so the
field is estimated again every time the kernel-weighted covariates change.

```{r fit-field, eval = FALSE}
fit_field <- multiScale_optim(start_field, inputs, n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r load-fit-field, include = FALSE}
fit_field <- field_cache$fit_field
# The stored fit leaves out its copy of the kernel inputs to stay small.
fit_field$kernel_inputs <- inputs
# A glmmTMB fit saved under one glmmTMB version must be rebuilt with up2date()
# before another version can use it. Newer versions add internal model terms.
fit_field$opt_mod <- glmmTMB::up2date(fit_field$opt_mod)
```

This search took about `r round(field_cache$fit_seconds / 5) * 5` seconds,
against less than one second without the field.

# Read the scales, the coefficients, and the field

```{r compare}
s_glm   <- summary(fit_glm)$opt_scale                     # sigma, SE, 95% CI (m)
s_field <- summary(fit_field)$opt_scale
b_glm   <- summary(fit_glm$opt_mod)$coefficients          # log-scale estimates
b_field <- summary(fit_field$opt_mod)$coefficients$cond

compare <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("sigma, land1 (m)", "sigma, land2 (m)", "intercept",
                "effect of site", "effect of land1", "effect of land2"),
  Truth     = c(250, 500, 1, 0.3, -0.5, 0.7),
  No_field  = c(s_glm[, "Mean"], b_glm[, "Estimate"]),
  SE        = c(s_glm[, "SE"], b_glm[, "Std. Error"]),
  Field     = c(s_field[, "Mean"], b_field[, "Estimate"]),
  SE_field  = c(s_field[, "SE"], b_field[, "Std. Error"]))
knitr::kable(compare, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "No field", "SE",
                           "With field", "SE"))
```

**How to read the table:** The first two rows are the scales of effect, in
meters. Without the field, the `land1` estimate is
`r val(round(s_glm["land1", "Mean"]))` m and its 95% interval
(`r val(round(s_glm["land1", "2.5%"]))` to `r val(round(s_glm["land1", "97.5%"]))` m)
misses the true 250 m. With the field, the estimate is
`r val(round(s_field["land1", "Mean"]))` m and the interval
(`r val(round(s_field["land1", "2.5%"]))` to `r val(round(s_field["land1", "97.5%"]))` m)
contains it. The remaining rows are on the log scale. The model without a field
overstates both landscape effects. It estimates that one standard deviation of
`land2` multiplies the expected count by
`r val(round(exp(b_glm["land2", "Estimate"]), 2))`, where the truth is
`r val(round(exp(0.7), 2))` and the field model gives
`r val(round(exp(b_field["land2", "Estimate"]), 2))`. Because the field model no
longer treats neighboring counts as independent, it also reports a larger
standard error for every coefficient.

```{r field-par}
# The field parameters, back-transformed from the log scale
field_par <- exp(glmmTMB::getME(fit_field$opt_mod, "theta"))
names(field_par) <- c("field SD (log scale)", "range (m)")
round(field_par, 2)

# K counts the regression coefficients, the field parameters, and the two sigmas
aic_tab(list(fit_glm, fit_field), mod_names = c("No field", "With field"))
```

**How to read the output:** The field standard deviation is on the scale of the
linear predictor, the log expected count. An estimate of
`r val(round(field_par[1], 2))` means that a location one standard deviation
above average has an expected count `r val(round(exp(field_par[1]), 2))` times
that of an average location with the same covariates. The range is in meters.
Correlation between two locations is `exp(-distance / range)`. With a range of
`r val(round(field_par[2]))` m it is
`r val(round(exp(-310.8 / field_par[2]), 2))` between neighboring survey points
and falls to 0.37 at `r val(round(field_par[2]))` m. The data were simulated
with a standard deviation of 0.6 and a range of 800 m. In the AICc table, lower
values mean better support, and the field model wins by a wide margin. Its `K`
is two larger because it adds the field standard deviation and the range.

> **What this means for your study.** One simulated data set shows what a field
> can change. It does not show that a field always improves a scale estimate.
> When the bundled counts, which have no residual spatial pattern, were fitted
> with the same field term, the field standard deviation was
> `r round(field_cache$bundled$field_par[1], 2)` and the scales barely moved
> (`r round(field_cache$bundled$sigma_field["land1", "Mean"])` and
> `r round(field_cache$bundled$sigma_field["land2", "Mean"])` m, against
> `r round(field_cache$bundled$sigma_glm["land1", "Mean"])` and
> `r round(field_cache$bundled$sigma_glm["land2", "Mean"])` m without it). Fit
> both models and compare them.

# Predict at the survey points

`predict()` returns the expected count. For a model with a field, you choose
whether the prediction includes the estimated field value at each location.

```{r predict-points}
# Default: includes the estimated field value at each survey point
p_field <- predict(fit_field, se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional")

# re.form = NA: sets the field to zero, leaving the covariate effects only
p_zero  <- predict(fit_field, re.form = NA)

round(head(data.frame(observed   = df$counts,
                      with_field = as.numeric(p_field$fit),
                      se         = as.numeric(p_field$se.fit),
                      field_zero = as.numeric(p_zero)), 5), 2)

# The estimated field at the survey points against the simulated one
cor(log(as.numeric(p_field$fit) / as.numeric(p_zero)), field)
```

**How to read the output:** `with_field` is the expected count at that survey
point, given what the counts revealed about the field there. `field_zero` is
the expected count for the same covariate values at a location where the field
equals zero. Treat it as a reference value, because it is not an average over
the field. The ratio of the two columns is the field's multiplier at that
point, and its log tracks the simulated field with a correlation of
`r val(round(cor(log(as.numeric(p_field$fit) / as.numeric(p_zero)), field), 2))`.

The standard error describes the expected count. It holds the estimated scales
of effect fixed and adds no observation noise. Request it with `se.fit = TRUE`
and `uncertainty = "conditional"`. Confidence limits (`interval = "confidence"`)
and joint uncertainty are not available for these fits, and `predict()` stops
with an error if you ask for them. The `prediction_contract` attribute of each
result records whether the field was included or set to zero.

# Predict at new locations and map the result

A new location needs its own kernel inputs and its own coordinates. Prepare
both, then set `allow.new.levels = TRUE` so that `glmmTMB` accepts positions it
did not see during fitting. Without that argument the call stops with an error
that names it and the alternative, `re.form = NA`.
At a new position, the field value is predicted from the field at the survey
points, weighted by the fitted correlation. Far from every survey point, the
prediction therefore returns to the zero-field value.

```{r predict-grid, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.8, fig.cap = "***Predictions on a 225 m grid inside the surveyed area.***"}
# A 225 m grid of new locations inside the surveyed area
grid_xy <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x = seq(800, 3500, by = 225),
                                 y = seq(800, 3500, by = 225)))
grid_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = vect(grid_xy, type = "points"),
                           raster_stack = land_rast, max_D = 1700,
                           kernel = "gaussian", bin = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

# One row per new location: site covariate, coordinates, and the field group
grid_dat <- data.frame(site = 0,
                       pos  = glmmTMB::numFactor(grid_xy[, 1], grid_xy[, 2]),
                       grp  = factor("all"),
                       row.names = rownames(grid_inputs$kernel_dat))

with_field <- predict(fit_field, grid_dat, grid_inputs,
                      allow.new.levels = TRUE,          # accept new positions
                      se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional")
no_field   <- predict(fit_field, grid_dat, grid_inputs, re.form = NA)

grid_map <- rast(data.frame(
  grid_xy,
  expected   = as.numeric(with_field$fit),
  multiplier = as.numeric(with_field$fit) / as.numeric(no_field),
  se         = as.numeric(with_field$se.fit)), type = "xyz")
plot(grid_map, nc = 3,
     main = c("Expected count", "Field multiplier", "Standard error"))
```

**How to read these plots:** The left panel is the expected count per survey
when `site` is zero, including the predicted field. The middle panel isolates
the field. A value above 1 marks an area where counts run higher than the
landscape covariates predict, and a value below 1 marks the opposite. The
right panel is the standard error of the expected count, in the same units.
Prediction time climbs steeply with the number of new positions (the 169 here
take a few seconds), so keep the grid coarse.

A map with the field set to zero can cover every raster cell. Prepare the
layers with `kernel_scale.raster()`, setting `scale_center = TRUE` and
`match_buffer = TRUE`, then call `predict()` with `re.form = NA`. This route
requires a raster with a projected coordinate reference system. It also expects
every variable in the model formula, so pass one fitted position and the group
label through `site_values`. With `re.form = NA` they do not change the result.

```{r predict-raster, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***Expected count from the covariate effects alone, with the field set to zero.***"}
# The bundled raster has no CRS. Declare a projected one, in meters.
map_rast <- land_rast
crs(map_rast) <- "EPSG:32617"

# Landscape layers at the estimated scales, with site held at zero. The field
# columns are placeholders that re.form = NA ignores.
layers <- kernel_scale.raster(
  map_rast, multiScaleR = fit_field,
  scale_center = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE, clamp = TRUE, verbose = FALSE,
  site_values = list(site = 0, pos = as.character(df$pos[1]), grp = "all"))
map_zero <- predict(fit_field, layers, re.form = NA)
plot(map_zero, main = "Expected count, field set to zero")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.4)
```

**How to read this plot:** Each cell holds the expected count that the
landscape covariates alone predict. Use this map to show the landscape effect,
and use the grid above when you want the best prediction for a place. Cells
near the border lie outside the surveyed area, so read them with caution.

# Current restrictions

Support for spatial fields is experimental. The package checks that its
predictions match those of `glmmTMB`. It has not yet evaluated how well scales
of effect are recovered, or whether intervals reach their nominal coverage,
when a field is present.

| Feature | Checked and supported | Not supported, or not checked |
|:--------|:----------------------|:------------------------------|
| Fitting | `multiScale_optim()` with the default `backend = "refit"` | The `profile_glm`, `joint_nb2`, and `joint_mixed` backends |
| Response | Gaussian. Poisson, negative binomial (`nbinom2`), and Gamma with a log link. Binomial with a logit link | Other families and links |
| Field | One field shared by all rows, with `exp()`, `gau()`, or `mat()` covariance | Several fields, or a field combined with other random effects |
| Coordinates | Projected, in the distance units of the raster | Longitude and latitude. Raster prediction stops without a projected CRS |
| Uncertainty | Sigma standard errors and intervals from `summary()`. Standard errors for predictions, with scales held fixed | Confidence limits and joint uncertainty from `predict()` |
| Held-out evaluation | `cross_validate_field()` for Gaussian responses with `exp()` or `gau()` covariance. It requires `glmmTMB` 1.1.14 and `TMB` 1.9.25 | Count and binomial responses |

`cross_validate_field()` fits a field model to part of the data and scores its
predictions for the rest, keeping all surveys from one location in the same
fold. See `?cross_validate_field` and
`vignette("v08-cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR")`.

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
# 1. Prepare kernel inputs and fit a baseline model without a field
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast, max_D = 1700,
                      kernel = "gaussian", bin = TRUE)
df <- data.frame(dat, inputs$kernel_dat)
start_glm <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)
fit_glm   <- multiScale_optim(start_glm, inputs, n_cores = 1)

# 2. Add a spatial field on the survey coordinates and estimate the scales
df$pos <- glmmTMB::numFactor(xy[, 1], xy[, 2])   # coordinates, in meters
df$grp <- factor(rep("all", nrow(df)))           # one field for all points
start_field <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  counts ~ site + land1 + land2 + exp(pos + 0 | grp),
  family = poisson(), data = df,
  start  = list(theta = c(log(0.5), log(500))))  # log field SD, log range (m)
fit_field <- multiScale_optim(start_field, inputs, n_cores = 1)

# 3. Read the results
summary(fit_field)$opt_scale                          # sigma, SE, interval (m)
summary(fit_field$opt_mod)$coefficients$cond          # log-scale coefficients
exp(glmmTMB::getME(fit_field$opt_mod, "theta"))       # field SD, range (m)
aic_tab(list(fit_glm, fit_field), mod_names = c("No field", "With field"))

# 4. Predict at the survey points, then at new locations
predict(fit_field, se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional")  # with the field
predict(fit_field, re.form = NA)                                # field at zero
predict(fit_field, grid_dat, grid_inputs, allow.new.levels = TRUE,
        se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional")   # grid_dat: site, pos, grp

# 5. Map the covariate effects with the field set to zero
layers <- kernel_scale.raster(
  map_rast, multiScaleR = fit_field,             # map_rast has a projected CRS
  scale_center = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE, clamp = TRUE,
  site_values = list(site = 0, pos = as.character(df$pos[1]), grp = "all"))
map_zero <- predict(fit_field, layers, re.form = NA)
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `glmmTMB::numFactor()` | Store survey coordinates in the form a `glmmTMB` covariance term needs |
| `glmmTMB::glmmTMB()` | Fit the starting model with an `exp()`, `gau()`, or `mat()` spatial field |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate the scales of effect, refitting the field at each candidate scale |
| `summary()`, `aic_tab()` | Report sigma with its interval, and compare models with and without a field |
| `predict()` | Expected response with the field (the default) or with the field at zero (`re.form = NA`) |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Apply the fitted kernels to a raster for mapping |
| `cross_validate_field()` | Score held-out predictions for a Gaussian response with a field |
